en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty Ninth Chapter
The Discussion on Bodily Action Not Being According to the Mind: Is it the case that bodily action does not conform to the mind?
Yes, it is.
Is there bodily action for one who is without contact? …pe… Is there bodily action for one who is without mind?
One should not say so …pe…
But is bodily action not that which possesses contact …pe… that which possesses consciousness?
Yes, it is.
If bodily action involves contact … and if bodily action involves the mind,
then indeed, it should not be said that "bodily action does not correspond to the mind."
Is bodily action not according to the mind?
Yes. Is there bodily action for one who does not turn [the mind], ...pe... for one who does not intend? Yes.
It should not be said so … [as before] … Is it not the case that for one who is turning back there is bodily action … pe … and for one who is directing the mind there is bodily action?
Yes, it is.
If there is bodily action for one who is turning back, and bodily action for one who is directing [the mind], then indeed, it should not be said:
"Bodily action does not correspond to the state of the mind.
Is it not the case that bodily action corresponds to the state of the mind?
“Yes.
“Is it not the case that bodily action is originated by mind, co-nascent with mind, and arises together with mind?
“Yes.”
If bodily action is originated by mind, co-nascent with mind, and arises simultaneously with mind, then surely it should not be said that "bodily action does not conform to the mind.
Is it not the case that bodily action conforms to the mind?

“Yes,” you say. “But would it not be the case that one who does not wish to advance does not advance; one who does not wish to retreat does not retreat; one who does not wish to look forward does not look forward; one who does not wish to look around does not look around; one who does not wish to contract [a limb] does not contract it; and one who does not wish to extend [a limb] does not extend it? It should not be said so… [and so on].

But surely, one who wishes to step forward steps forward; one who wishes to step back steps back; one who wishes to look ahead looks ahead; one who wishes to look around looks around; one who wishes to bend a limb bends it; one who wishes to stretch a limb stretches it? Yes.
Indeed, one who wishes to step forward steps forward... [and so on].
If one who wishes to stretch out [a limb] stretches it out, then surely it should not be said:
"Bodily action does not conform to the mind.
It should not be so said.
“Is it not the case that bodily action does not always follow the mind?”—
“Yes.”—
“But is there not someone who, intending ‘I will go elsewhere,’ goes elsewhere... [and so on]”?
“If one thinks, ‘I will stretch out another [limb],’ and then stretches out another [limb]?”—
Yes. If it is so that someone, thinking, “I will go elsewhere,” goes elsewhere …pe… [the same applies].
“If one extends another [limb] thinking, ‘I shall extend another,’ then indeed, O sir, it must be said:
‘Bodily action is not in accordance with the mind.
The discussion on the point that bodily action is not in accordance with the mind is concluded.
